title: The cell and cell organelles
definition: A cell is the smallest unit of life that can exist on its own and perform all the activities needed to keep a living thing alive. Every plant, animal, fungus, and microorganism is made up of one or more cells, and within each cell there are tiny working parts called organelles. The term "organelle" simply means "little organ," because each part has a special job, just as the heart and lungs have special jobs in our body. In Class 6, you study six important cell parts: the cell wall, the cell membrane, plastids, the nucleus, the vacuole, and the cytoplasm. A plant cell and an animal cell share many of these parts, but they are not identical. A plant cell has a rigid cell wall outside the cell membrane. This wall is made mainly of cellulose and gives the plant its shape and support, which is why a tree or a neem stem can stand tall without bones. Just inside the wall is the cell membrane, a thin, flexible barrier that controls what enters and leaves the cell. It is like a security gate that allows useful substances such as water, oxygen, and nutrients to come in, while keeping harmful substances out. The cytoplasm is the jelly-like substance that fills the space between the cell membrane and the nucleus; all the organelles float in it, and many important chemical reactions happen here. The nucleus is the large, dark, usually round body near the center of the cell. It is the control center because it contains the instructions that direct all cell activities, including growth and reproduction. Plastids are small structures found mostly in plant cells. The most important plastids are chloroplasts, which contain the green pigment chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis to make food from sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide. Some plastids called chromoplasts give bright colours to flowers, fruits, and roots such as the orange colour of a carrot or the red of a ripe tomato. The vacuole is a large, fluid-filled sac. In plant cells it is especially big and stores water, dissolved nutrients, and waste products. Because of the water it holds, the vacuole also helps keep the plant firm and upright. When labelling a plant cell diagram, you should be able to show the cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, large central vacuole, and plastids including chloroplasts. When labelling an animal cell diagram, you should show the cell membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, and small vacuoles; you must not draw a cell wall or large plastids. Remembering the exact structure and function of each organelle, and being able to tell a plant cell from an animal cell, is the main goal of this topic.
textWalkthrough:
This is the very first node on the cell for Class 6, so there is no earlier node you must recall before starting. Think of it as opening a new door into biology. The first thing to keep in mind is that a cell is not just a tiny blob; it is a busy factory where each organelle has a specific task.

Let us begin with the outer coverings. Have you ever noticed that a plant does not collapse even when it grows very tall? That is because of the cell wall. The cell wall is a rigid, non-living layer found outside the cell membrane in plant cells. It is made of a substance called cellulose. A good answer about the cell wall would say, "The cell wall is a tough outer layer made of cellulose in plant cells; it gives shape, support, and protection to the cell." A weak answer would only say, "It is the outer part of the cell," because that misses both the material and the function. Animal cells do not have a cell wall, which is why our body cells are more flexible.

Just inside the cell wall, or at the very edge of an animal cell, lies the cell membrane. This is a thin, living membrane made mainly of proteins and lipids. Its main work is to control the entry and exit of substances. Imagine a school gatekeeper who checks every person going in or out. Water, useful salts, and food can enter; wastes can leave; but harmful substances are stopped. A strong answer explains both the structure and the role of control.

Now think about the inside of the cell. The cytoplasm is the jelly-like, semi-fluid substance in which all the organelles are suspended. It is not empty space; many reactions happen here. If a diagram asks you to label the cytoplasm, look for the shaded or granular area between the cell membrane and the nucleus.

The nucleus is usually the largest, darkest, round or oval structure inside the cell. It is called the control center because it controls all cell activities, including growth and division. It contains the hereditary material. A common way to remember this is to compare the nucleus to the manager's office in a factory; from there, instructions are sent to every worker.

Next come plastids. These are tiny, coloured bodies found mainly in plant cells. Chloroplasts are the most important plastids for Class 6. They contain chlorophyll and make food by photosynthesis. If you look at a slide of a Hydrilla or Elodea leaf under a microscope, you can see green chloroplasts moving inside the cells. Chromoplasts are another type of plastid; they give colour to parts like the red skin of a tomato or the yellow of a marigold flower. You do not need to describe endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi bodies, or lysosomes here because they are not in this syllabus point.

The vacuole is a large, water-filled sac. In plant cells it is very big and centrally placed. It stores water, food, and waste, and because it is full of liquid it helps keep the plant stiff. On a hot day, if a plant loses too much water, the vacuole shrinks and the plant wilts. Animal cells have small, temporary vacuoles or none at all.

Let us also compare plant and animal cells clearly. A plant cell has a cell wall, a large vacuole, and plastids such as chloroplasts. An animal cell has no cell wall, no large permanent vacuole, and no plastids. Both have a cell membrane, cytoplasm, and a nucleus.

For the ICSE board exam, questions on this topic are usually straightforward but require precise language. Examiners expect you to name the organelle, describe its structure, and state its function in one or two neat sentences. They also expect correct labelling of diagrams. A common examiner concern is that students confuse terms or give vague definitions; so always use the exact words from the syllabus such as "rigid outer layer," "controls entry and exit," "control center," "jelly-like substance," and "storage." Practice drawing and labelling both diagrams neatly, because a well-labelled diagram can score full marks.
eli5: A cell is like a tiny bag full of jelly called cytoplasm. Around it is a thin skin called the cell membrane. Plant cells have a stiff wall outside that skin. Inside the cell there is a bossy ball called the nucleus that tells the cell what to do. Green specks called chloroplasts make food from sunlight. A big water balloon called the vacuole stores water and keeps the plant stiff.
misconceptionText:
1. Confusing the cell wall and the cell membrane: Many students write that the cell membrane gives support to the plant. This is incorrect. The cell wall is the rigid outer layer that gives shape and support; the cell membrane is the thin, flexible covering that controls entry and exit. The board examiner observations note that candidates often confused similar terms, such as writing "vasectomy" instead of "tubectomy" or making spelling errors like "Tubecotomy." The same kind of mix-up happens in cell biology when students swap "cell wall" and "cell membrane." Always remember: wall comes first and is stiff; membrane is inside and is the gatekeeper.

2. Saying that all organelles are found in both plant and animal cells: Some students add a cell wall, a large vacuole, or plastids to an animal cell diagram. This is wrong. Animal cells do not have a cell wall or plastids, and their vacuoles are small and temporary. The exam guidance show that students often give incorrect statements, such as confusing one process with another. Similarly, confusing plant-only structures with animal cell structures shows that the fundamentals have not been mastered.

3. Writing vague or incomplete functions: A weak answer might say, "The vacuole stores things." A correct answer should say, "The vacuole is a large, fluid-filled sac that stores water, dissolved nutrients, and waste products, and it helps keep the plant cell firm." The board exam guidance remind teachers to "review topic fundamentals" because common errors arise from partial recall. Always give both the structure and the function.
diagnosticText:
Q1 (recall): Name the six cell organelles studied in this topic and state one function of each.
Answer: The six cell organelles are the cell wall, the cell membrane, plastids, the nucleus, the vacuole, and the cytoplasm. The cell wall is a rigid outer layer found in plant cells; it is made of cellulose and gives the cell shape, support, and protection. The cell membrane is a thin, flexible covering that controls the entry and exit of substances into and out of the cell. Plastids are small structures found mainly in plant cells; chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis to make food from sunlight, and chromoplasts give colour to flowers and fruits. The nucleus is the control center of the cell because it contains the instructions that direct all cell activities, including growth and division. The vacuole is a large, fluid-filled sac that stores water, dissolved nutrients, and waste products, and in plant cells it also helps keep the cell firm. The cytoplasm is the jelly-like substance in which all the organelles are suspended and in which many chemical reactions occur.

Q2 (reasoning): A student looks at two slides under the microscope. Slide A has cells with a thick outer layer, large green structures, and a big central water-filled space. Slide B has cells with a thin outer border, no green structures, and no large water-filled space. Which slide shows a plant cell, and how can you tell?
Answer: Slide A shows a plant cell. A plant cell has a thick, rigid cell wall made of cellulose outside the cell membrane, which gives it a firm outer layer. It also contains plastids, such as chloroplasts, which are green because they contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis. In addition, a plant cell has a large central vacuole that is filled with cell sap, which stores water, nutrients, and waste. Slide B shows an animal cell because it only has a thin, flexible cell membrane at the outer edge, it lacks a cell wall, it has no green plastids, and its vacuoles are small and temporary. The three key differences are therefore the cell wall, plastids, and the large central vacuole. If the student simply saw the outer layer and guessed, the answer would be weak; a strong answer uses all three structural clues together.

Q3 (evaluate): A student says, "Plant and animal cells are exactly the same because both have a cell membrane, cytoplasm, and a nucleus." Is this statement correct? Give a balanced argument.
Answer: This statement is only partly correct. It is true that plant and animal cells are similar in several ways. Both have a cell membrane that controls what enters and leaves, a cytoplasm in which the organelles float, and a nucleus that acts as the control center. These shared features remind us that all living cells have a common plan. However, the statement is also incorrect because plant and animal cells have important differences. A plant cell has a rigid cell wall made of cellulose outside the cell membrane, while an animal cell has no cell wall. A plant cell has large, permanent plastids, especially chloroplasts for photosynthesis, whereas an animal cell has no plastids. A plant cell also has one large central vacuole that helps keep it firm, but an animal cell has only small, temporary vacuoles or none at all. Therefore, the two kinds of cells are similar in basic structure but different in important details, and the statement must be rejected as fully correct.

Q4 (apply): Your teacher asks you to draw and label an animal cell. You must also explain why you should not draw a cell wall or large plastids in it. How would you answer?
Answer: In an animal cell diagram, I would label the cell membrane, the cytoplasm, the nucleus, and possibly one or more small vacuoles. I would not draw a cell wall because animal cells do not have a rigid cellulose wall; only plant cells have this protective and supportive layer. I would not draw large plastids or chloroplasts because plastids, especially green chloroplasts, are found mainly in plant cells that perform photosynthesis. Animal cells cannot make their own food from sunlight, so they do not need chloroplasts. If I added a cell wall to an animal cell, the diagram would be marked wrong. A neat, correctly labelled diagram with clear boundaries and correct spelling of each label would help me score full marks in the board exam.

Q5 (create): Imagine that you are the manager of a tiny cell factory. Assign one job to each of the six organelles you have learned and explain how they work together to keep the factory running.
Answer: In my cell factory, the cell wall is the strong outer boundary wall that keeps the building from collapsing, especially in the plant branch. The cell membrane is the security gate that checks everything entering or leaving, allowing in raw materials and sending out finished products and waste. The cytoplasm is the factory floor, a jelly-like workspace where all the machines are placed and where the actual work happens. The nucleus is the manager's office; it stores all the instructions and sends orders to the rest of the factory so that every worker knows what to do. The plastids, especially chloroplasts, are the solar power units that capture sunlight and turn it into food or energy for the factory. The vacuole is the storage tank that holds water, nutrients, and waste until they are needed or removed. Together, these six organelles form a complete working system: the wall and membrane protect and control the factory, the cytoplasm provides the working space, the nucleus gives directions, the plastids provide energy, and the vacuole stores supplies. If any one of them stops working, the whole cell factory would be in trouble.
masteryCriteria: Can define a cell as the basic unit of life; can name and state one function of five organelles (nucleus: control, cell membrane: boundary, cytoplasm: jelly, mitochondria: energy, vacuole: storage); can draw and label a simple cell.

title: Plant vs animal cell differences
definition: A cell is the smallest unit of life, and although all living cells share certain basic parts, plant cells and animal cells are not built exactly the same way. In Class 3 you learned that living things grow, move, reproduce, and need food and water; now, in Class 6, you are learning that these life processes depend on tiny structures inside cells called organelles. The most important differences between a typical plant cell and a typical animal cell are three in number, and each difference has a special significance that helps the organism survive. First, a plant cell is surrounded by a rigid cell wall outside the cell membrane, while an animal cell has only a flexible cell membrane and no cell wall. The cell wall is made chiefly of a substance called cellulose, and it gives the plant cell a fixed, box-like shape and provides mechanical support to the entire plant. Without this wall, a plant would not be able to stand upright. Second, plant cells contain plastids, especially chloroplasts, which are green organelles that carry out photosynthesis, the process by which plants make their own food using sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide. Animal cells do not contain chloroplasts and therefore cannot make their own food; they must obtain food from outside. Third, plant cells usually have one or a few large, permanent vacuoles that can occupy up to 90 percent of the cell volume and store water, food, and waste. This large vacuole helps maintain turgor pressure, keeping the plant firm and stiff. Animal cells, by contrast, have small, temporary vacuoles, if they have them at all. Other parts such as the nucleus and cytoplasm are present in both cell types. When you compare the two cells in a table, you must remember that the wall, chloroplasts, and vacuoles are the three clear marks that distinguish a plant cell from an animal cell.
textWalkthrough:
In Class 3, you studied that living things show certain common features such as growth, movement, reproduction, and the need for food and water. You could observe these features directly in plants and animals around you. Now, in Class 6, you are moving from those outside observations to the inside of the organism, where you learn that the features of living things have a cellular basis. In this node we are going to compare plant and animal cells, and the comparison will make sense only if you already know the main organelles found in each type of cell.

This is why your immediate prerequisite, node c6_bio_010, is so important. In that node you studied the main cell organelles and what each one does. You must remember that plant cells and animal cells both have a cell membrane, cytoplasm, and a nucleus, but that plant cells also possess a cell wall, plastids, and large vacuoles. If you try to compare the two cells without first naming these parts, your answer will remain vague and you may lose marks. So, before continuing, quickly recall from c6_bio_010: the cell wall is a stiff covering outside the plant cell membrane; plastids such as chloroplasts are green bodies that make food; and the vacuole is a large fluid-filled space inside the plant cell.

Let us now walk through the three key differences one by one. The first difference is the cell wall. A plant cell has a thick, rigid cell wall outside the thin cell membrane. This wall is made of cellulose and gives the plant cell a definite shape. Because each plant cell is like a tiny box, many such boxes pressed together give strength and support to stems, leaves, and roots. An animal cell has no cell wall; it is covered only by a flexible cell membrane. This is why an animal cell can change its shape, like a soft balloon. A good way to understand the significance is to think of a cardboard box. If you pack soft items inside a box, the box keeps its shape and protects what is inside. In the same way, the cell wall keeps the plant cell stiff and protects it.

The second difference is the presence of plastids, particularly chloroplasts, in plant cells. Chloroplasts contain a green pigment called chlorophyll and are the sites where photosynthesis takes place. During photosynthesis, the plant uses sunlight, carbon dioxide from the air, and water from the soil to prepare food in the form of glucose. This is why plants are called autotrophs, or self-feeders. Animal cells do not have chloroplasts and cannot make their own food. They are heterotrophs, which means they must eat plants or other animals to obtain nutrition. Without chloroplasts, animals could not survive on sunlight alone.

The third difference is the size and number of vacuoles. A plant cell usually has one very large, permanent central vacuole filled with cell sap. This vacuole stores water, salts, sugars, and sometimes waste products. When the vacuole is full of water, it presses against the cell wall and makes the plant firm and upright. This state is called turgidity. If the plant does not get enough water, the vacuole shrinks and the plant wilts. Animal cells have only small, temporary vacuoles that appear and disappear quickly, often used for storing or transporting substances for short periods.

Let us now compare a good answer with a weak answer. A weak answer might simply say, "Plant cells have a wall and animal cells do not." A good answer says, "A plant cell is surrounded by a rigid cellulose cell wall outside the cell membrane, which gives it a fixed shape and supports the plant, whereas an animal cell has only a flexible cell membrane and can change its shape." Similarly, a weak answer for chloroplasts might state, "Plants are green." A good answer explains that plant cells contain green chloroplasts in which photosynthesis occurs, while animal cells lack chloroplasts and cannot make their own food. For vacuoles, a weak answer says, "Plant cells have big vacuoles." A good answer adds that the large central vacuole stores water and maintains turgor pressure, while animal cells have small, temporary vacuoles.

In the ICSE board examination, questions on this topic are usually direct and of low to medium difficulty. You may be asked to give any three differences between plant and animal cells, or to explain the significance of any one difference. Examiners expect the answer in a neat comparative tabular form with three clearly stated points: the presence or absence of the cell wall, the presence or absence of plastids or chloroplasts, and the nature of the vacuoles. Always mention the significance, because merely listing the difference is not enough. Practice drawing a neat table with columns for plant cell, animal cell, and significance, and your answer will meet the examiner's expectations.
eli5: Imagine a plant cell as a tiny green box. It has a hard wall outside, little green kitchens inside that make food using sunlight, and a big water balloon that keeps it stiff. An animal cell is more like a soft jelly ball. It has no hard wall, no green kitchens, and only tiny water bubbles. These three things make plant and animal cells different.
misconceptionText:
Misconception 1: Confusing the cell wall with the cell membrane. Some students write that both plant and animal cells have a cell wall. In reality, the cell wall is present only in plant cells, outside the cell membrane. Animal cells have only a cell membrane. The board exam guidance for 2024 note that candidates often confuse similar-sounding terms such as centrosome, centromere, and centriole. This tells us that biology students at this level frequently mix up terms that look or sound alike. To avoid this error, always remember: the membrane is thin and flexible and is present in all cells; the wall is thick, rigid, and present only in plant cells.

Misconception 2: Thinking that animal cells are larger than plant cells or that plant cells have no vacuoles at all. Some students also confuse the drawings of plant and animal cells in the examination and interchanged their labels. This matches the CISCE 2023 examiner observation that candidates were confused between the types of cells and interchanged them incorrectly, identifying figures as the L.S. of a leaf and swapping the characteristic features. The correction is to look for the three clear markers: the cell wall for plant cells, the chloroplasts for plant cells, and the large central vacuole for plant cells. If the diagram shows a regular shape with a thick outline and a large empty space in the middle, it is a plant cell.

Misconception 3: Believing that all green parts of a plant contain chloroplasts. While green leaves and young green stems contain chloroplasts, roots and some non-green parts usually do not. However, for the purpose of comparing a typical plant cell with an animal cell, remember that the presence of chloroplasts is a general feature of plant cells, not animal cells. A common error in the board exam analysis was that candidates used related but incorrect terms such as "photolysis" and "polymerisation" instead of "photophosphorylation" when describing photosynthesis. Although that exact term is beyond Class 6, the lesson is that you should use the correct words your syllabus gives you, such as chloroplast, photosynthesis, and chlorophyll, and not replace them with confusing terms.
diagnosticText:
Q1 (recall): List any three differences between a plant cell and an animal cell and state the significance of each difference.
Answer: The first difference is that a plant cell has a rigid cell wall made of cellulose outside the cell membrane, while an animal cell has no cell wall and is covered only by a flexible cell membrane. The significance is that the cell wall gives a fixed shape to the plant cell and provides support and protection, enabling the plant to stand upright. The second difference is that a plant cell contains plastids, especially chloroplasts, which have a green pigment called chlorophyll, while an animal cell lacks plastids and chlorophyll. The significance is that chloroplasts enable the plant to carry out photosynthesis and make its own food using sunlight, water, and carbon dioxide. The third difference is that a plant cell has one or more large, permanent vacuoles that store water, food, and waste, while an animal cell has only small, temporary vacuoles, if any. The significance is that the large vacuole in the plant cell helps maintain turgor pressure and keeps the plant firm and upright; when it loses water, the plant wilts.

Q2 (reasoning): Why does a plant cell need a cell wall and a large vacuole, while an animal cell can manage without them?
Answer: A plant cell needs a cell wall because plants cannot move from place to place and must remain standing in one position throughout their life. The cell wall provides mechanical strength and a fixed shape to each cell, and thousands of such rigid cells together support the entire plant against gravity and wind. A plant cell also needs a large vacuole because it must store water for long periods, especially when the soil may become dry. A full vacuole presses the cytoplasm against the cell wall and keeps the cell turgid, which is why a well-watered plant looks stiff and upright. An animal cell does not need a cell wall because animals can move and change shape; their flexible cell membrane allows them to bend, crawl, and take in food by processes such as phagocytosis. Animal cells also do not need a large permanent vacuole because their cells are surrounded by a circulating fluid environment that provides water quickly, and their small temporary vacuoles are enough for short-term storage and transport of materials.

Q3 (evaluate): A student says, "The cell wall is not important because the cell membrane alone can protect the cell." Do you agree or disagree? Give reasons for your answer.
Answer: I disagree with this statement because the cell wall has a very important role that the cell membrane cannot perform alone. The cell membrane is a thin, flexible layer that controls what enters and leaves the cell, but it is not strong enough to give shape or support to a tall plant. The cell wall, on the other hand, is a thick, rigid layer made of cellulose that lies outside the cell membrane in plant cells. It gives the plant cell a definite shape and provides mechanical strength. This is why plants such as the neem tree, the banyan tree, or a sunflower can grow tall and stand upright without falling. If only the cell membrane were present, the plant cells would be soft like animal cells and the plant would collapse. However, the statement does contain a small truth: the cell membrane is still important for protection in its own way because it forms a barrier between the cell and the outside environment and regulates the movement of water, food, and waste. But the cell wall is not unimportant; it is essential for the rigidity and support of plant cells. Therefore, the student's view is incorrect, and both the cell wall and the cell membrane have their own special and necessary functions.

Q4 (apply): Look at the following list of features and identify which belong to a plant cell, which belong to an animal cell, and which belong to both: cell wall, chloroplast, large permanent vacuole, small temporary vacuole, cell membrane, nucleus, cytoplasm, ability to carry out photosynthesis.
Answer: Features that belong to a plant cell are the cell wall, chloroplast, large permanent vacuole, and the ability to carry out photosynthesis. The cell wall is a thick, rigid covering made of cellulose that gives shape and support. The chloroplast is the green organelle that contains chlorophyll and is the site of photosynthesis. The large permanent vacuole stores water and helps maintain turgor pressure. Features that belong to an animal cell are the small temporary vacuole, which may appear for short-term storage and transport. Features that belong to both plant and animal cells are the cell membrane, nucleus, and cytoplasm. The cell membrane is the thin, flexible outer covering that controls the movement of substances in and out of the cell. The nucleus is the control centre that contains genetic material and directs all cell activities. The cytoplasm is the jelly-like substance inside the cell in which all the organelles are suspended and many chemical reactions take place. Therefore, both cells share the basic machinery of life, but the plant cell has the extra structures that allow it to stand upright and make its own food.

Q5 (create): Imagine you are a science reporter for your school magazine. Write a short paragraph in which you compare a plant cell to a cardboard box, an animal cell to a soft balloon, a chloroplast to a kitchen, and a vacuole to a water bottle. Explain which comparison fits best and why.
Answer: A plant cell is like a cardboard box because it has a hard, rigid cell wall on the outside that keeps its shape and protects the softer parts inside, just as a cardboard box keeps its shape and protects whatever is packed within it. An animal cell is like a soft balloon because it has only a thin, flexible cell membrane and can change its shape, just as a balloon can be squeezed and still return to shape. A chloroplast is like a tiny green kitchen because it uses sunlight as fuel and turns simple ingredients such as water and carbon dioxide into food for the plant, just as a kitchen turns raw ingredients into a meal. A vacuole is like a water bottle because it stores a large amount of water, and when it is full the plant becomes stiff and firm, just as a filled water bottle stands upright. The best comparison is that of the plant cell to a cardboard box because it directly shows why the cell wall is important: without the box-like wall, the plant cell would not have a fixed shape and the plant could not stand. The comparison of the chloroplast to a kitchen is also strong because it makes the process of photosynthesis easy to understand for a young reader.
masteryCriteria: Can state three differences between plant and animal cells (cell wall: plant only, chloroplast: plant only, vacuole size: large in plant, small in animal); can identify a cell as plant or animal from a diagram.

title: Unicellular and multicellular organisms
definition:
The living world is built from tiny units called cells, and the number of cells an organism possesses is one of the simplest ways to classify it. A unicellular organism is a complete living thing made of just one cell. That single cell is the entire organism: it must capture or make food, breathe, move, grow, respond to stimuli, excrete wastes, and reproduce -- all within the same microscopic boundary. Classic examples include Amoeba, which appears as a shapeless blob under the microscope and changes its form constantly; Paramecium, a slipper-shaped protist covered with tiny hair-like cilia; Chlamydomonas, a green, single-celled alga commonly found in freshwater puddles and ditches; and even the far smaller bacteria and yeast that are single-celled and invisible without strong magnification. Because a unicellular organism has no separate tissues or organs, its one cell carries every life process and each part of the cell performs multiple functions.

In contrast, a multicellular organism is made of many cells that are usually organised into tissues, organs, and organ systems. A human being, a mango tree, a rose bush, an earthworm, and a cat are all multicellular. In these organisms, different groups of cells become specialised for particular jobs: some cells form the covering layer, others contract to produce movement, still others conduct food and water, and many are devoted to protection or reproduction. This specialisation is possible because the cells cooperate and show a division of labor. For example, in the human body, red blood cells transport oxygen, nerve cells carry messages, and muscle cells bring about movement. In a mango tree, root hair cells absorb water, leaf cells carry out photosynthesis, and xylem cells transport water upward. The key difference between the two kinds of organisms is therefore not simply the number of cells, but how life processes are managed. In a unicellular organism, one cell does everything; in a multicellular organism, many specialised cells work together so that the organism as a whole can live, grow, and reproduce more efficiently.

Some students wonder whether a colony of cells, such as Volvox, counts as a multicellular organism. A true colony is a group of similar cells living together, but the individual cells may still be quite independent. This is different from a multicellular organism, in which cells are specialised and depend on one another. The concepts of unicellular and multicellular organisms are the first step toward understanding why larger, more complex organisms need different tissues and why the cell is truly the basic unit of life.
textWalkthrough:
Let us begin where you already are. In Class 3, you learned that all living things grow, reproduce, and carry out life processes such as feeding, breathing, moving, and responding to changes around them. That was node c3_bio_001, and it gave you the big idea: living things share common features. Now, in Class 6, we are going to take that idea one step deeper. We ask: can one tiny cell really do all of those life processes by itself, or does an organism need many cells working together? That is the question this node, c6_bio_012, answers.

Before we can answer it, we need to be sure we remember what a cell actually is. That is why node c6_bio_010, the cell as the basic unit of life, is the direct prerequisite here. Once you know that a cell is the smallest living unit that can carry out all life activities, it becomes clear why some organisms are called single-celled and others many-celled. Think of the cell as a brick. A one-brick building is small and simple, but the same brick can also be one of millions in a huge, complex building.

Let us look at the one-brick building first. A unicellular organism has only one cell, but that one cell is alive in the full sense of the word. It feeds, breathes, grows, responds, excretes, and reproduces. Amoeba is an excellent example. If you place a drop of pond water on a glass slide and view it under a microscope, you may see Amoeba as a tiny, colourless, ever-changing blob. It has no fixed shape because it pushes out finger-like projections called pseudopodia. That same single cell catches food, digests it, removes wastes, and divides to produce new Amoebae. Paramecium is another common example from pond water; it is slipper-shaped and swims using tiny hair-like cilia. Chlamydomonas is a single-celled green alga that you might find in freshwater tanks or puddles after rain. Even the bacteria and yeast that you cannot see without a microscope are single-celled. So the word "unicellular" means "one cell," and it describes organisms in which that one cell is the whole living thing.

Now let us think about the many-brick building. A multicellular organism contains many cells. These cells are not all the same; they become specialised for different jobs. This specialisation is called division of labor. In a human being, for example, some cells become nerve cells that carry messages, some become muscle cells that help us move, some become blood cells, and some form the protective skin. In a mango tree, which you may see all across India from Maharashtra to West Bengal, root cells absorb water and minerals, leaf cells make food by photosynthesis, and wood cells give support. The human being and the mango tree are both complete organisms, but they are made of millions of specialised cells working in cooperation.

It is useful to compare good and weak answers here. The idea of tissues -- groups of similar cells doing a particular job -- is reserved for Class 7, but it is good to remember that multicellularity is more than just many cells stuck together.

Examples of unicellular organisms are Amoeba, a shapeless protozoan found in pond water that moves by forming pseudopodia, and Paramecium, a slipper-shaped ciliated protozoan. Other common unicellular organisms are Chlamydomonas, a green alga, bacteria, and yeast. A multicellular organism, on the other hand, is made up of many cells that are usually organised into tissues and organs. These specialised cells perform different functions, showing a division of labor. Q2 (reasoning): A student says, "A unicellular organism cannot be complete because it has only one cell." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
Answer: This statement is incorrect because a unicellular organism is a complete organism even though it is made of a single cell. The single cell is able to carry out all the life processes that keep the organism alive. For example, Amoeba uses its cell membrane and pseudopodia to capture food particles, digests the food inside food vacuoles, removes waste materials, responds to changes in its surroundings, grows in size, and finally divides into two daughter Amoebae to reproduce. Similarly, Paramecium swims with cilia, takes in food through an oral groove, and reproduces by fission. Because the cell contains all the necessary structures and organelles, the organism does not need separate tissues or organs. A cell is the basic unit of life, and in unicellular organisms, one cell is the whole living thing. The presence of many cells is not required for an organism to be complete; it is the ability to perform life processes that makes it a true organism.

Q3 (evaluate): "All organisms that live in groups or colonies are multicellular." Evaluate this statement with a balanced argument.
Answer: This statement is not entirely correct and needs careful evaluation. On one hand, many multicellular organisms do live in groups or show social behaviour. However, living in a group is not the same as being multicellular. A multicellular organism is made of many cells that are specialised for different functions and are usually organised into tissues and organs. In contrast, some organisms form colonies made of many similar cells that are not specialised. For example, Volvox forms a spherical colony of many green algal cells, but the individual cells are mostly alike and can often survive on their own. This is a colony of unicellular organisms, not a true multicellular organism. On the other hand, a sponge or a human being is truly multicellular because its cells are specialised -- some for protection, some for movement, some for transport, and some for reproduction. Therefore, the statement is false if it is meant as a definition. Living in a colony does not automatically make an organism multicellular. The correct criterion is the presence of many specialised cells that show division of labor and cooperation, not simply the number of cells gathered together or their habit of living in groups.

Q4 (apply): Look at the following list of organisms: Amoeba, Paramecium, Chlamydomonas, human being, mango tree, bacteria, yeast, and ant. Classify each as unicellular or multicellular, and explain the basis of your classification.
Answer: The organisms can be classified as follows. In a human being, cells are organised into tissues such as blood, muscle, and nerve tissue. In a mango tree, cells are specialised to form roots, leaves, stems, and flowers. In an ant, different cells form the body wall, digestive system, muscles, and nerves. The basis of classification is the number of cells and, more importantly, whether the organism shows division of labor among specialised cells or whether a single cell carries out every life process.

Q5 (create): Imagine you are a single-celled organism living in a drop of pond water. Write a short diary entry describing how your one cell manages a complete day of feeding, moving, responding to danger, and reproducing.
Answer: Dear Diary, today began with the warm morning light reaching my pond. I am an Amoeba, and my whole body is just one cell. To find food, I pushed out parts of my cell body to form pseudopodia and surrounded a tiny bit of algae. The food was enclosed in a food vacuole inside me, and my cell slowly digested it. When the water became too warm, I moved away to a cooler corner by changing my shape and flowing in that direction. That is how I respond to stimuli. I do not have legs or muscles; my one cell does all the moving. I also removed waste materials through my cell membrane. As the day ended, I grew a little larger and then divided into two daughter Amoebae. Each daughter is a complete organism, just like me. title: Tissue concept and plant meristematic tissue
definition:
A tissue is a group of similar cells that are arranged together and work as a team to carry out one particular function in a living organism. In the study of plants, tissues are broadly classified into two main types: meristematic tissues and permanent tissues. Meristematic tissue is made up of living cells that are constantly dividing. These cells have thin cell walls, a dense cytoplasm, a large and prominent nucleus, and very small or no vacuoles. Because they keep dividing, they help the plant to grow in length and thickness. The permanent tissues, on the other hand, are formed when meristematic cells stop dividing and become specialised to perform a particular function. This process of change from meristematic cells into permanent cells is called differentiation.

Meristematic tissue is of three main types based on its location in the plant. The apical meristem is found at the growing tips of roots and shoots and is responsible for the increase in length of the plant. The lateral meristem, which includes the cambium, is found along the sides of stems and roots and helps in the increase in the girth or thickness of the plant. The intercalary meristem is located at the nodes of stems, especially in grasses and other monocots, and helps in the elongation of the internodes. A key point to remember is that meristematic tissue gives rise to permanent tissue. As long as the cells keep dividing, they remain meristematic. Once they stop dividing and take up a specific job, they become permanent tissue. This is a very important idea because it connects the two tissue types.

We can also compare meristematic and permanent tissues clearly. Meristematic cells are living, thin-walled, densely cytoplasmic, and have a large nucleus. They keep dividing and have no specialisation. Permanent cells are those that have stopped dividing and have taken on a definite structure and function. Some permanent cells are living, like parenchyma, and some are dead, like sclerenchyma, depending on their function. In everyday language, one could say that meristematic tissue is like a factory that keeps producing new bricks, while permanent tissue is like the wall that is already built using those bricks. Examples of meristematic tissue include the tips of growing roots, the tips of shoots, and the cambium layer in the stem. Understanding the tissue concept is the first step in learning how the bodies of plants are organised, and it builds directly on the earlier learning that the cell is the basic unit of life.

We ask: what happens when many similar cells group together to do one particular job? The answer is a tissue.

Imagine a school. Each student is like a cell. When a group of students come together to form a football team, each player has a specific role, but they all work towards one goal. A tissue is just like that team: a group of similar cells performing a specific function. The word similar is important. The cells in a tissue are not random; they are alike in shape and function. Their walls are thin, their cytoplasm is dense, and their nucleus is large. They are found at places where the plant is actively growing. The apical meristem sits at the tips of roots and shoots, like a cap at the end of a pencil. It pushes the plant upward and downward. If you look at a grass stem, you may not see it, but the intercalary meristem at the nodes helps the stem to grow taller rapidly. A weak answer would simply list the names without explaining the connection.

Q1 (recall): Define the term tissue and name the two main types of plant tissues.
Answer: A tissue is a group of similar cells that are organised together to perform a specific function. In plants, tissues are mainly of two types: meristematic tissue and permanent tissue. Meristematic tissue is made up of cells that are living, thin-walled, densely cytoplasmic, and contain a large nucleus. These cells keep dividing continuously. Permanent tissue is formed from meristematic tissue when the cells stop dividing and become specialised for a particular function. For example, the cells in the apical meristem keep dividing to make the plant grow taller, while permanent tissues such as parenchyma or sclerenchyma provide support, storage, or other functions. The two types are connected because meristematic tissue gives rise to permanent tissue through the process of differentiation.

Q2 (reasoning): Explain why meristematic cells have thin walls, dense cytoplasm, and a large nucleus. How do these features help the cell in its function?
Answer: Meristematic cells are specialised for rapid and repeated cell division. Their thin walls make it easy for the cell to expand and divide without much resistance. The dense cytoplasm shows that the cell is metabolically very active because it needs a lot of energy and building material to make new cells. The large nucleus is important because it contains the chromosomes and controls all the activities of the cell, including cell division. If the vacuoles are large, they would take up too much space and slow down the process of division, so meristematic cells have very small or no vacuoles. In short, every feature of a meristematic cell supports its main job: continuous division and the production of new cells for plant growth.

Q3 (evaluate): "Permanent tissues are more important than meristematic tissues in a plant because they do the actual work, while meristematic tissues only keep dividing." Evaluate this statement.
Answer: This statement is only partly true and needs careful evaluation. Permanent tissues are certainly important because they carry out the actual functions of the mature plant. For example, parenchyma stores food, sclerenchyma gives support, and xylem transports water. Without these tissues, the plant cannot survive as a complete organism. However, it is not correct to say that meristematic tissues are less important just because they keep dividing. In fact, without meristematic tissue, permanent tissues would never be produced in the first place. Meristematic cells are the source of all new cells, and through differentiation they become the permanent cells that do the work. Both types are therefore equally important, but at different stages of the plant's life. Meristematic tissue is responsible for growth and the production of new cells, while permanent tissue is responsible for the day-to-day functions of the plant body. A balanced view is that meristematic and permanent tissues are complementary. One produces new cells, the other uses those cells for specific jobs. Neither can replace the other. A good answer in the board exam would recognise this balance and not choose one side blindly.

Q4 (apply): A gardener noticed that the stem of a bamboo plant grew very quickly after the rainy season. Which type of meristematic tissue is mainly responsible for this rapid growth, and where would you find it in the stem? Give one other example of a plant where the same type of meristem helps it to grow taller quickly.
Answer: The rapid growth of the bamboo stem is mainly due to the intercalary meristem. This type of meristematic tissue is located at the nodes of the stem, and it helps in the rapid elongation of the internodes. Bamboo and grasses are classic examples where the intercalary meristem is very active, allowing the plant to grow quickly in height. Another example is sugarcane, which also grows tall rapidly because of the intercalary meristem present at the nodes. It is important not to confuse this with the apical meristem, which is at the tip and helps in the overall length of the root or shoot, or the lateral meristem, which increases the thickness of the stem. In the board exam, you should clearly name the tissue, state its location, and connect it to the example given in the question.

Q5 (create): Imagine you are a tiny observer travelling inside a plant. Describe the journey of a meristematic cell from the time it is formed in the apical meristem until it becomes a permanent cell in a mature part of the plant.
Answer: I begin my journey at the tip of a young root, inside the apical meristem. All around me, cells are small, living, and busy dividing. The cytoplasm is thick and the nucleus is large. I am one of these meristematic cells, and my only job is to keep dividing. As new cells are produced, some of us are pushed away from the tip. Slowly, I stop dividing. My wall becomes thicker and my shape changes. I develop a large central vacuole. This change from a dividing cell to a specialised cell is called differentiation. Now I have become a permanent cell. If I am in the storage tissue, I may store food like starch. If I am in the support tissue, my wall may become thick and strong. No matter where I end up, I am now part of the permanent tissue that keeps the plant working. My journey shows the wonderful story of growth: cells divide, they move, they change, and they take up specific functions to build the plant body.

title: Plant permanent tissues (parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma)
definition:
Simple permanent tissues are the mature, specialized tissues that originate from meristematic tissues when their cells lose the ability to divide and take on particular roles in the plant body. In the ICSE Class 7 syllabus, we focus on three ground tissues--parenchyma, collenchyma, and sclerenchyma--each with a characteristic structure, position, and job.

Parenchyma is the most abundant and versatile simple permanent tissue. Its cells are living, with thin cell walls made mainly of cellulose and large intercellular spaces that allow the exchange of gases and storage. You find parenchyma in the pith and cortex of stems and roots, in leaves, and in the pulp of fruits such as the fleshy mango. When parenchyma cells contain chloroplasts, they are called chlorenchyma and carry out photosynthesis; when they have large air spaces to help floating plants breathe, as in lotus stems or water hyacinth, they are called aerenchyma. The chief functions of parenchyma are storage of food, water, and nutrients, photosynthesis in chlorenchyma, and giving a certain amount of support to softer plant parts.

Collenchyma is also living, but its cells show thickening of cellulose and pectin at the corners. These corner thickenings give it strength while the thin primary wall between the corners keeps it bendable. Collenchyma is found in leaf stalks, in the periphery of young stems, and in the stems of climbers such as gourd and pea, allowing them to flex in the wind without snapping. It provides flexibility and mechanical support to growing plant organs.

Sclerenchyma consists of dead cells at maturity. Their cell walls are heavily thickened and lignified, meaning the tough substance lignin has been deposited; this makes the wall hard and impermeable, and the cells have almost no intercellular spaces. Fibres and sclereids are two forms. Sclerenchyma occurs in the veins of leaves, the hard coverings of seeds and nuts, and the husk of the coconut. It gives strength, rigidity, and protection.

To compare the three: parenchyma is alive, thin-walled, and loose; collenchyma is alive, corner-thickened, and flexible; sclerenchyma is dead, uniformly thick and lignified, and rigid. Together they illustrate the great principle that the same starting cells--meristematic cells--can differentiate into tissues beautifully fitted for storage, flexibility, or strength.

But what happens when these cells stop dividing and settle into a job? That is exactly where this lesson begins. A meristematic cell can become a permanent cell, and when many such permanent cells work together, they form a simple permanent tissue. So before you call a tissue 'permanent,' you must remember that it has come from actively dividing meristematic cells that have now specialized.

Let us start with parenchyma, the tissue you probably see most often. If someone asks, 'Which simple permanent tissue stores food and has thin cell walls?' a good answer is not just the word 'parenchyma.' A weak answer might say, 'It is a soft tissue in fruits.' A strong answer explains: parenchyma cells are living, have thin cellulose walls and large intercellular spaces, and are found in leaves, stems, roots, and the pulp of fruits such as a juicy mango. When parenchyma contains chloroplasts, it is called chlorenchyma and performs photosynthesis; when it has large air spaces, it is called aerenchyma and helps aquatic plants like lotus and water hyacinth float and breathe. Next comes collenchyma. Picture the stem of a climbing gourd or pea plant swaying in a strong monsoon wind. Why does it bend instead of breaking? The answer lies in collenchyma. Its cells are living, but their corners are thickened with cellulose and pectin. This corner thickening gives the tissue just enough strength to hold the plant upright while the thinner portions between the corners let the organ bend. A poor response would be, 'It is a thick tissue that supports the plant,' because that sounds like sclerenchyma. Now consider sclerenchyma. Look at the hard coconut husk from the coconut groves of Kerala, the shell of a tamarind seed, or the tough veins in a dried leaf. These parts contain sclerenchyma, a tissue made of dead cells whose walls are heavily thickened and lignified. Lignin is a hard, waterproof substance that makes the wall rigid. That is wrong: it has no intercellular spaces, the cells are dead at maturity, and its job is strength and rigidity, not storage or bending. A good answer contrasts it clearly: 'Sclerenchyma has thick, lignified walls, no intercellular spaces, and gives strength and rigidity to parts such as the veins of leaves and the husk of coconut.'

Are there large or no intercellular spaces? What is the location and the function? Parenchyma is like a soft storehouse; collenchyma is like a bendable yet firm rod; sclerenchyma is like a hard wooden shell.

Finally, in the ICSE Board examination, examiners expect you to not only name the tissue but also explain how its structure suits its function. They often notice that students either mix up the three tissues or give vague descriptions such as 'it helps the plant' or 'it gives support to all parts.' Avoid that by giving the precise tissue, its cell-wall structure, and one Indian example. If a diagram shows a stem, leaf, or seed, look for the clues--thin walls and big spaces for parenchyma, corner thickenings for collenchyma, thick lignified walls for sclerenchyma--and you will write with the confidence of a student who has traced each tissue from its meristematic origin to its permanent role.

However, the rest of the wall remains thin and the cells are usually loosely arranged, so the tissue can bend without breaking. This is very important for young stems and leaf stalks, especially in climbers such as gourd, pea, and bean, which need to sway in the wind and move towards supports. If the entire wall were thick and lignified like sclerenchyma, the stem would be rigid and brittle; if the walls were uniformly thin like parenchyma, the stem would be too weak. The corner thickening of collenchyma is therefore a perfect middle path: it gives the strength of extra wall material exactly where it is needed, while leaving the sides flexible enough to allow bending. So, whenever you see a plant part that must stay up yet move, remember collenchyma.

Parenchyma is a living, thin-walled tissue with large intercellular spaces. It is the main storage tissue for food, water, and nutrients; the potato tuber, the pulp of mango, and the pith of stems all depend on it. In the form of chlorenchyma, parenchyma carries out photosynthesis, the very process that produces the food that keeps the plant--and, ultimately, the animal world--alive. In aquatic plants, parenchyma as aerenchyma provides buoyancy and oxygen transport. Collenchyma too has its own role: it gives flexibility and mechanical support to young and growing organs that still need to elongate and bend. Therefore, the three simple permanent tissues are not in competition. They are a team. Sclerenchyma is more important for rigidity, parenchyma for storage and photosynthesis, and collenchyma for flexible support. The most accurate view is that each tissue is important in the right place and at the right stage of growth. A strong plant with no food storage would starve; a plant full of stored food with no strength would collapse. So the statement should be balanced to say that sclerenchyma is crucial for strength and rigidity, but parenchyma and collenchyma are equally essential for the plant's survival and growth.

Q4 (apply): A student is shown three plant specimens: a soft mango fruit, a flexible green stem of a climbing gourd, and a hard coconut husk. Name the simple permanent tissue likely to be dominant in each specimen and give one reason for your choice.
Answer: In the soft mango fruit, the dominant simple permanent tissue is parenchyma. The fleshy pulp consists of living cells with thin cell walls and large intercellular spaces; these cells store water, sugars, and food, giving the fruit its soft, juicy texture. In the flexible green stem of a climbing gourd, collenchyma is the main support tissue. The cells are living, and their corners are thickened with cellulose and pectin; this arrangement gives the young stem enough mechanical strength to stay upright while still allowing it to bend and sway. In the hard coconut husk, sclerenchyma is the dominant tissue. Its cells are dead at maturity and have thick, lignified walls with no intercellular spaces; the deposition of lignin makes the wall hard and waterproof, providing the rigidity and protection seen in the husk. Thus, by matching the structure and texture of the specimen to the structure and function of the tissue, the student can correctly identify parenchyma in the fruit, collenchyma in the young flexible stem, and sclerenchyma in the hard husk. This is the kind of practical reasoning the ICSE examiner expects in diagrams and application questions.

Q5 (create): Design a simple working model or a classroom demonstration that compares the three simple permanent tissues. Describe the materials you would use and how the model shows structure and function.
Answer: For a classroom demonstration I would build a three-part model on a wooden board. The parenchyma model would be a soft sponge cut into small cubes with gaps between them. The sponge cubes represent living, thin-walled parenchyma cells, and the air gaps between them are the large intercellular spaces. I would press a little coloured water into the sponge to show that it can store water and food, just as parenchyma stores starch and water in fruit pulp. For collenchyma, I would take a bundle of plastic straws and wrap tape thickly only at the points where they touch, leaving the rest of each straw free. The taped joints represent cellulose and pectin corner thickenings, while the free straw walls show the flexible thin parts that let the stem bend. I would then bend the bundle to show that it stays upright yet does not snap. For sclerenchyma, I would use small wooden blocks glued tightly together without gaps and painted brown. The blocks stand for dead, thick, lignified cells with no intercellular spaces. I would try to press or bend the wooden block and show that it does not give way, proving strength and rigidity. Finally, I would label each part and invite a classmate to pull or press each model, so the difference between storage, flexible support, and rigid strength becomes easy to feel and remember.
masteryCriteria: Can name parenchyma, collenchyma, and sclerenchyma and state one feature of each (thin-walled, thickened corners, thick dead walls); can give one function of each (storage, flexibility, strength); can identify each from a diagram.

title: Complex permanent tissues (xylem and phloem)
definition: A complex permanent tissue is a plant tissue that is built from more than one kind of cell, with these different cells working together as a single functional unit. The two chief examples you will meet in Class 7 are xylem and phloem, and together they form the vascular bundle, the plant's transport system. Xylem is a complex permanent tissue made up of four kinds of cells: tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres. Tracheids and vessels are the tracheary elements; they are long, tube-like, dead cells whose lignified walls give them both strength and the ability to conduct water and dissolved minerals from the roots upward to the stems and leaves. Because they are dead at maturity, they do not block the flow, and their thick walls prevent them from collapsing. Xylem parenchyma, on the other hand, is made of living cells that store food and water and help the tissue to function as a whole. Xylem fibres are thick-walled, dead mechanical cells that give support to the plant. Phloem is the second complex permanent tissue. It is also made of four kinds of cells: sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma and phloem fibres. The sieve tubes and companion cells are living, with the companion cells providing energy and control to the sieve tube elements, which themselves have only a thin film of cytoplasm and usually lack a nucleus. Phloem parenchyma stores food, while phloem fibres give mechanical support and are dead. The function of phloem is the transport of prepared food, mainly sugars, from the leaves, where it is made, to all other living parts of the plant; this movement is called translocation. Unlike xylem, which carries water and minerals only upward from the roots, phloem can move food in different directions, so its transport is bidirectional. This is why xylem and phloem are called complex tissues: each is composed of several different cell types that are specialised for different jobs but cooperate as one transport system. Xylem and phloem are easily told apart by what each carries: xylem carries water and minerals, and phloem carries food.
textWalkthrough:
Think back to what you learned in Class 6, in node c6_bio_010: the cell is the basic unit of life. That idea is still with you, but now you are taking the next step. In Class 7 you have already studied simple permanent tissues in node c7_bio_002, where a tissue is made of only one kind of cell. Parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma each have a single cell type doing one job. Today we move from that to something more elaborate. If one kind of cell can form a tissue, what happens when several kinds of cells must work together? That is exactly the idea behind a complex permanent tissue, and the two great examples are xylem and phloem.

Let us begin with the simplest question: what makes xylem and phloem complex? A tissue is called complex not because it is difficult, but because it is made of different kinds of cells. Each cell type has its own shape and its own special task, yet they all act as one unit. In xylem, the main conducting cells are the tracheids and vessels. These are the tracheary elements. Picture them as microscopic water pipes. A tracheid is a long, tapering cell with pits, while a vessel is made of several short cells called vessel elements stacked on top of one another to form a long open tube. Both are dead at maturity, with lignin deposited in their walls, so they are strong enough to support the plant and allow water to move freely through them. Living water-conducting cells would slow the flow, so the plant removes the cell contents to turn these cells into hollow channels. The other two members of xylem, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres, are not the main conductors. Xylem parenchyma is living and stores food and water; xylem fibres are thick-walled, dead support cells. In a good answer you would say that most cells of xylem are dead except for the parenchyma. A weak answer would only say that xylem carries water and forget the mineral part, or would confuse tracheids with vessels. Tracheids are not the same as vessels: tracheids are shorter and imperforate at the ends, while vessels have open ends and a wider lumen, making them faster water conductors.

What does xylem actually transport? It carries water and dissolved mineral salts from the roots to all other parts of the plant. This movement is generally upward, from the soil into the root, up the stem, and into the leaves. Imagine a tall coconut palm in Kerala or a banyan tree in the Indian Botanic Garden at Howrah. The water that reaches every leaf at the top has travelled through xylem. This is conduction, and it is a one-way flow because the leaves lose water by transpiration and the roots absorb more from the soil. A common mistake is to say that xylem carries food too, or to say that it can move water up and down. It does not; xylem is for water and minerals only, and the direction is upwards.

Now turn to phloem. Here the conducting cells are quite different. The sieve tubes are the food channels. Each sieve tube is a column of living sieve tube elements whose end walls have tiny pores, like the holes in a kitchen sieve. The companion cells lie next to the sieve tubes and are living cells with a nucleus and many mitochondria. They provide energy and help to load and unload sugars into the sieve tube. Phloem parenchyma stores food, and phloem fibres, like xylem fibres, give mechanical support and are dead. In a good answer you would remember that sieve tubes and companion cells are living, whereas xylem vessels and tracheids are dead. A weak answer would say that all phloem cells are living, or that sieve tubes are dead like vessels. That is wrong because the living companion cells keep the sieve tube alive.

The function of phloem is translocation: the transport of prepared food, mostly sucrose and other sugars, from the leaves to all other living parts of the plant. This food may go upward to the growing buds of a neem tree in Rajasthan, downward to the roots of sugarcane in the fields of Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra, or sideways into a developing fruit. That is why phloem is called bidirectional. Its movement is not fixed in one direction. A helpful image is to think of xylem as a one-way water pipe rising up a building, while phloem is a food delivery service that can travel both ways depending on where the food is needed.

Finally, why do we call xylem and phloem complex permanent tissues? They are complex because each contains several different cell types, and they are permanent because, once formed, these cells do not divide. They are also called vascular tissues because they together form the vascular bundle, the plant's transport network. When the CISCE board examiner asks this, you should be ready to give a labelled diagram, list the cells of each tissue, and explain the difference in transport. Examiners expect you to use the correct terms and to be specific about what each cell type does; they are not satisfied with vague statements such as xylem carries water and phloem carries food. Learn the four components of each tissue, the living or dead condition of each, and the direction of transport, and you will be fully prepared.
eli5: Xylem is like a one-way water pipe inside a plant. It takes water and minerals from the roots up to the leaves. Phloem is like a food delivery truck. It takes sugar made in the leaves to every other part of the plant, and it can go up or down. Both are made of many kinds of cells, so they are called complex tissues.
misconceptionText: The board exam guidance often point out that students confuse one term with another because they learn words by sound rather than by meaning. In the same way, many Class 7 students mix up xylem and phloem. One very common error is to say that xylem transports food. This is wrong. Xylem transports only water and minerals, and the movement is from the roots upward. If you say that xylem carries sugar from leaves, you have described phloem, not xylem. A second error is to believe that all cells in both xylem and phloem are living. The truth is different. In xylem, the tracheids, vessels and xylem fibres are dead at maturity; only the xylem parenchyma is living. In phloem, the sieve tubes and companion cells are living, but the phloem fibres are dead. A third frequent mistake is to think that xylem carries water both up and down. It does not. Xylem conduction is mainly upward, while phloem transport, called translocation, can move food in different directions and is therefore bidirectional. The examiner observations remind teachers to make students list the different parts clearly and say exactly what each one does, so always name the cell types rather than speaking in general terms.
diagnosticText:
Q1 (recall): Name the four kinds of cells found in xylem and the four kinds of cells found in phloem. Also state which of these cells are living and which are dead.
Answer: Xylem contains tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres. The tracheids and vessels are the tracheary elements that conduct water and minerals. They are dead at maturity because they lose their protoplasm and become hollow, lignified tubes. Xylem parenchyma is living; its cells store food and water and help the tissue to function. Xylem fibres are also dead and serve as support cells. Phloem, on the other hand, contains sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma and phloem fibres. The sieve tubes are living though they lack a nucleus at maturity; the companion cells are fully living and lie beside the sieve tubes to provide energy and help load food. Phloem parenchyma is living and stores food. Phloem fibres are dead and give mechanical strength to the tissue. Therefore, in xylem most of the conducting and mechanical cells are dead, with only parenchyma remaining alive, whereas in phloem the sieve tubes and companion cells are the living conducting cells.

Q2 (reasoning): Why are xylem and phloem called complex permanent tissues? Give two reasons for each name.
Answer: Xylem and phloem are called complex tissues because each is made of more than one kind of cell that works together as a single functional unit. Xylem has four different cell types, and phloem also has four different cell types, so neither of them is built from a single repeated cell in the way a simple permanent tissue is. They are called permanent tissues because, once these cells are formed and differentiated, they lose the ability to divide and remain in the same mature state throughout their life. The word permanent also reminds us that these tissues are meant for a fixed function rather than for growth by division. Thus, the name complex permanent tissue combines two ideas: several cell types working together and a mature, non-dividing condition. This is why the study of simple permanent tissues in the previous node is such an important stepping stone; it gives you the contrast of one cell type against which the many cell types of xylem and phloem become clear.

Q3 (evaluate): A student writes in an answer: "Phloem transports water and dissolved minerals from the roots to the leaves, and it is made only of dead cells like the vessels of xylem." Evaluate this statement.
Answer: The student's statement is incorrect in several ways. First, the function of phloem is not to transport water and dissolved minerals. That is the job of xylem, which carries water and minerals from the roots to all aerial parts of the plant. Phloem transports prepared food, mainly sugars, from the leaves to all other living parts of the plant; this process is called translocation. Second, the student has also mixed up the direction of movement. Xylem conduction is generally upward, while phloem movement is bidirectional, meaning it can carry food from a source such as a mature leaf to a sink such as a growing bud, a root, or a fruit, which may lie in any direction. Third, the student is wrong in saying that phloem is made only of dead cells like vessels. Sieve tubes are living cells, although they have lost their nucleus, and the companion cells that lie beside them are fully living cells with a nucleus and many mitochondria. Phloem parenchyma is also living, while only phloem fibres are dead. The vessels and tracheids of xylem are indeed dead, but that fact does not apply to phloem. The correct view is therefore: phloem carries food, not water and minerals; phloem transport is bidirectional, not upward only; and phloem contains living sieve tubes and companion cells as well as dead fibres.

Q4 (apply): A student places the roots of a potted balsam plant into a solution of red ink for a few hours. After cutting the stem, she finds red streaks in the lower part of the stem and the leaf veins. Explain why this happens and name the tissue responsible.
Answer: The red streaks appear because the ink dissolved in the water has been absorbed by the roots and then carried up through the stem and into the leaf veins. The tissue responsible is the xylem. Xylem is a complex permanent tissue made of tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres. The water-conducting cells, the tracheids and the vessels, are dead at maturity and form hollow, lignified tubes that run continuously from the roots to the leaves. When the roots take in the red ink solution, it moves along with the water and dissolved minerals through these xylem channels by conduction. Because xylem transport is mainly upward, the ink accumulates in the lower and middle portions of the stem and then spreads into the leaf veins through the vascular bundles. This is the reason the experiment is used in schools to show the path of water conduction. It does not stain phloem because phloem carries food and is not involved in moving water from the roots.

Q5 (create): Design a simple school-level experiment to show that phloem carries food from a leaf to other parts of the plant and moves in more than one direction.
Answer: Take a potted money-plant or any leafy herb growing in sunlight. Choose one mature leaf that is well exposed to light and paint the upper surface of that leaf with dilute iodine solution after it has been in the sun for a few hours, or use a radioactive or coloured tracer that is taken up by the leaf if one is available. Leave the plant in bright light for the next two to three hours. After that, cut thin sections of the stem both above and below the treated leaf and observe them under a microscope or test for the presence of the tracer. If the phloem carries food away from the treated leaf, the tracer should appear in the phloem of the stem both above and below the leaf. This is because phloem transport is bidirectional: food can move from the leaf upward to growing buds or downward to the roots, depending on where the food is needed. To make the experiment reliable, use a control plant with no treatment and test it in the same way. This comparison shows that the movement is due to the treated leaf, not to some other process. The experiment demonstrates that phloem, not xylem, is the food-conducting tissue and that its transport is not limited to one direction.
masteryCriteria: Can define xylem (transports water and minerals upward) and phloem (transports food in both directions); can name one cell type in each (xylem vessels, phloem sieve tubes); can distinguish between xylem and phloem function.
